items.stem: Using your knowledge of the law, "There is no longer any need for separate professions of solicitors and barristers." Discuss.
items.answer: For: overlapping roles: solicitor-advocates, direct access to barristers; fusion could reduce costs to clients; duplication of work. Against: barristers provide specialist advocacy; cab-rank rule protects access to justice; small firms can access specialist barristers without employing them. Conclusion: The professions are converging, but there are still benefits in a specialist independent Bar.

items.stem: Ethan, aged 17, has received a summons for jury service at Lisbon Crown Court. Ethan is currently on bail for a theft charge. Advise Ethan whether Ethan can or must serve on the jury. Explain the relevant legal rules before applying them.
items.answer: Law: Juries Act 1974: aged 18-75, on the electoral register and resident in the UK for at least five years since age 13; disqualified: those on bail, those with certain sentences (five years or more for life; any custody or community order in the last ten years) and mentally disordered persons; excusal and deferral are discretionary; police officers and lawyers are eligible since the CJA 2003. Application: Ethan is 17; jurors must be 18-75; Ethan is currently on bail for a theft charge, so Ethan is disqualified while on bail. Conclusion: If within the age range, Ethan is disqualified while on bail; anyone outside 18-75 cannot serve.

items.stem: Judge Samuel is due to hear a case involving an environmental charity. It emerges that the judge is an unpaid director of a charity linked to one of the parties. Advise whether Judge Samuel should hear the case. Refer to at least one decided case.
items.answer: Law: judges must be impartial and independent; a judge must not sit if there is a real possibility or appearance of bias (Pinochet (No 2) 1999); judges take an oath to act without fear or favour. Application: because the judge is an unpaid director of a charity linked to one of the parties, a fair-minded observer could think there is a real possibility of bias; as in Pinochet, the decision could be set aside if the judge sits. Conclusion: Judge Samuel should declare the interest and not hear the case.

items.stem: Describe the selection and appointment of lay magistrates.

items.stem: Describe how jurors are selected for a Crown Court trial.
items.answer: Names are chosen at random from the electoral register by the Jury Central Summoning Bureau; those summoned may be excused or have service deferred; at court a panel is chosen by ballot and 12 are sworn in, subject to challenges for cause and the prosecution's right to stand by.

items.stem: Kenji, aged 76, has received a summons for jury service at Lagos Crown Court. Kenji is currently on bail for a theft charge. Advise Kenji whether Kenji can or must serve on the jury. Refer to at least one decided case.
items.answer: Law: Juries Act 1974: aged 18-75, on the electoral register and resident in the UK for at least five years since age 13; disqualified: those on bail, those with certain sentences (five years or more for life; any custody or community order in the last ten years) and mentally disordered persons; excusal and deferral are discretionary; police officers and lawyers are eligible since the CJA 2003. Application: Kenji is 76; jurors must be 18-75; Kenji is currently on bail for a theft charge, so Kenji is disqualified while on bail. Conclusion: If within the age range, Kenji is disqualified while on bail; anyone outside 18-75 cannot serve.

items.stem: "There is no longer any need for separate professions of solicitors and barristers." Discuss.
items.answer: For: overlapping roles: solicitor-advocates, direct access to barristers; fusion could reduce costs to clients; duplication of work. items.stem: Using your knowledge of the law, evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using juries in criminal trials.
items.answer: For: public confidence and participation; jury equity (Ponting); random selection reduces bias; secrecy allows free discussion. Against: jurors may not understand complex evidence; racial or other bias (Mirza); internet research and social media (Fraill); jury tampering (Twomey); perverse verdicts and no reasons given. Conclusion: Juries are an important democratic safeguard, though reforms such as better guidance on the internet are needed.
